semantic_correction.stem: The spouse caring for a client with advanced cancer says, 'I am sleeping only a few hours, missing work, and I am afraid I will make a mistake with the medications because I am exhausted.' Which nursing action is most appropriate?

options.A: Assess the caregiver's current demands, available resources, and ability to perform care safely, then help arrange task-sharing, respite, social-work, or counseling support as needed.
options.B: Encourage the spouse to continue the current caregiving routine independently for now, because accepting outside help may make adjustment to the caregiver role more difficult.
options.C: Normalize the severe exhaustion as part of advanced-cancer caregiving and focus on medication teaching, with additional support considered only if an actual error occurs.
options.D: Focus the visit on the client's symptoms and treatment plan, and defer the spouse's sleep loss, work strain, and caregiving stress to a separate nonclinical setting.

semantic_correction.rationale: A is correct. Current National Cancer Institute guidance defines caregiver burden as stress or strain that occurs when caregiving demands exceed the resources available to the caregiver. NCI notes that caregivers may have emotional, social, financial, employment, health, and caregiving-task needs, and that clinicians should recognize caregiver roles, responsibilities, challenges, and support needs. NCI guidance encourages caregivers to ask for and accept help, share tasks, use counseling or social-work resources when useful, and consider respite care so they can rest and maintain their own health. In this scenario, severe sleep loss, missed work, and fear of making medication errors indicate that caregiving demands may exceed available resources and may affect safe home care. The nurse should therefore assess the caregiver's capacity and current resources and help arrange individualized practical and psychosocial support. B is incorrect because NCI specifically encourages accepting help and sharing responsibilities rather than assuming the caregiver should manage alone. C is incorrect because severe exhaustion and concern about medication errors warrant assessment and support before an error occurs. D is incorrect because caregiver well-being and ability to carry out care are clinically relevant components of cancer care and should not be excluded from the plan.
semantic_correction.educational_objective: Recognize significant caregiver burden when caregiving demands exceed available resources and respond by assessing caregiver capacity and safety and linking the family with individualized task-sharing, respite, social-work, counseling, or other support resources.
semantic_correction.source_organization: National Cancer Institute (NCI), National Institutes of Health

semantic_correction.source_locator: Informal Caregivers in Cancer HP PDQ → Caregiver Burden: burden is perceived when caregiving demands exceed available resources; Secondary Appraisal: Resources for Informal Caregivers includes recognition of caregiver responsibilities/challenges, guidance for caregiving tasks, information, and support in coping; Interventions include counseling, problem solving, skill building, psychoeducation, and supportive therapy. Patient Version → caregivers have emotional, social, financial, employment, and self-care needs; burden occurs when demands are greater than available resources; home-health support may reduce burden. Taking Care of Yourself → Ask for Help from Others and Use respite care: caregivers often wish they had asked for help sooner, should share tasks and seek support, and may use respite so they can rest and attend to their own needs.
semantic_correction.source_claim_supported: Current NCI guidance directly supports recognizing caregiver burden when demands exceed resources, assessing caregiving capacity and needs, and using task-sharing, respite, social-work, counseling, peer, and other support resources to protect caregiver well-being and safe care.

semantic_correction.correction_summary_append: RULE1 cleanup: removed the absolute-word and correct-answer length cues, rebuilt all four nursing actions to comparable length and specificity, freshly verified current NCI caregiver-burden and respite guidance, and made caregiver-capacity assessment plus individualized support the single best response before a safety error occurs.

audit_findings_append.source_locator: Informal Caregivers in Cancer — caregiver burden/resources/interventions; Taking Care of Yourself — ask for help and respite care
audit_findings_append.blueprint_locator: Psychosocial Integrity — family coping, support systems, and therapeutic communication
audit_findings_append.finding: The revised item tests recognition and management of significant cancer-caregiver burden with one clearly best nursing action, balanced alternatives, current NCI guidance, and no absolute-word or answer-length cue.

option_audit.A: Correct. It identifies the mismatch between caregiving demands and available resources, assesses safety and capacity, and uses practical and psychosocial supports supported by NCI guidance.
option_audit.B: Incorrect. NCI encourages accepting help and sharing responsibilities rather than requiring exhausted caregivers to continue independently.
option_audit.C: Incorrect. Severe sleep loss and concern about medication errors warrant assessment and support before an actual error occurs rather than normalization.
option_audit.D: Incorrect. Caregiver strain and ability to perform home-care tasks safely are clinically relevant to the cancer plan and should not be deferred outside care.

ambiguity_check: No second defensible answer. A uniquely combines caregiver-capacity assessment, safety, and individualized resource linkage; B reinforces unsupported self-reliance, C delays care until harm occurs, and D excludes a clinically relevant caregiver issue.
cueing_check: All four options are parallel nursing actions of comparable length and specificity; the prior 'all'/'only' distractors and uniquely-long correct response were removed.
